citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Washington)
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. It consists of multiple-choice questions where a model must choose the most sensible solution to a physical goal from two options. The dataset contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with additional development and test sets, inspired by instructables.com and designed to test knowledge of physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation.
name: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations. Annotators were required to pass a qualification HIT with >80% accuracy before participating in the main annotation task.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low annotator agreement were removed from the data. Human performance was calculated by majority vote on development data, with annotators chosen from those who achieved 90% on the qualification HIT. Human accuracy was measured at 94.9% on the validation set.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable page as inspiration and asked to provide: (1) a physical goal, (2) a valid solution, and (3) a "trick" — a subtly incorrect solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation stage; annotators had to achieve >80% accuracy on well-formed and underspecified (goal, solution) pairs to participate. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. A diff button was included in the interface to highlight differences between solutions, improving annotator accuracy and speed. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr.
rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was identified as a key challenge: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are most often drawn to prototypical solutions and look for tools in the kitchen (e.g., forks and knives) or the garage (e.g., hammers and drills), rarely considering the hundreds of other everyday objects. To address this, annotators were prompted with instructables links to encourage out-of-the-box thinking and flatten the distribution of referenced objects. AFLite was applied to remove stylistic artifacts and annotation artifacts that could artificially inflate model performance.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected via crowdsourcing using Amazon Mechanical Turk (HITs). Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com pages and asked to: (1) construct a physical goal, (2) provide a valid solution, and (3) provide a "trick" — a subtly incorrect solution that sounds plausible. Annotators were seeded with instructables drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions and project pages from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for activities including cooking, car repair, crafting, and home projects. These served as inspiration prompts for annotators to construct goal-solution pairs.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Crowdsourcing
rai:dataLimitations: Examples requiring expert-level knowledge of a domain (e.g., special woodworking terminology) were removed during validation as they do not fall under "commonsense." The dataset focuses on human-generated tricks, meaning annotators were free to come up with clever ways to hide deception, sometimes making very subtle changes (as little as one word difference). The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Models trained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance, but this would not necessarily indicate true physical understanding.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was applied to remove annotation artifacts and trivial examples. AFLite uses 5,000 examples to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of all remaining instances, then uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets to identify instances whose embeddings are strongly indicative of the correct answer. Such instances are discarded to reduce spurious biases. Examples with low annotator agreement during validation were also removed. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense, which is critical for building language models useful beyond NLP — including robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world to eventually be communicated with language, and PIQA is intended to highlight the gap between current language-only models and true physical understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. The dataset can also be used as a diagnostic tool to probe the physical knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, and to study which aspects of physical commonsense (e.g., object affordances, spatial relations, temporal relations) are captured by language representations.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm using BERT-Large fine-tuned on 5,000 examples to compute embeddings for bias detection and removal. SpaCy tokenizer used for tokenizing goals and computing statistics. GPT BPE tokenizer used for analyzing solution length distributions.
